Simulation-based power and design analysis for a two-group Gaussian design

Source: R/power.R
power_design.Rd

Estimate power by repeatedly simulating from the specification and applying a two-sample t-test, alongside the Type S (sign) and Type M (magnitude) design-analysis errors of Gelman and Carlin (2014).

Usage

power_design(
  spec,
  n_sims = 1000,
  alpha = 0.05,
  workers = 1,
  cl = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less")
)

Arguments

spec

A design specification (path or list) for a two-group Gaussian design with one row per subject (see Details).

n_sims

Number of Monte Carlo replicates. A power estimate carries a Monte Carlo standard error of about sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_sims), reported as power_mcse, and type_s and type_m average over the significant replicates alone, so they settle more slowly still. At least 200 replicates are advisable for study planning.

alpha

Significance level of the test, two-sided unless alternative says otherwise.

workers

Number of local worker processes over which to spread the replicates. The default of 1 runs serially. Because every replicate takes its own seed from replicate_seeds(), any worker count returns results identical to a serial run.

cl

A cluster made by parallel::makeCluster() to run the replicates on, in place of one started for this call, in which case workers is ignored. The cluster is left running for its owner to stop, and through sweep_spec() one cluster serves every grid point.

alternative

The test's alternative hypothesis: "two.sided", the default, or "greater" or "less" for a one-sided test of a directional prediction (see Details).

Value

A list with elements n_sims, alpha, alternative, power, power_mcse (its Monte Carlo standard error), power_lo and power_hi (its 95% Wilson interval), n_significant, true_effect and mean_estimate. Then come type_s (sign-error rate among significant replicates), type_s_lo and type_s_hi (its 95% Wilson interval), type_m (mean exaggeration ratio among significant replicates) and type_m_mcse (its Monte Carlo standard error). Both design-analysis quantities are NaN when no replicate reached significance and when the true effect is zero, as in the null condition design_conditions() produces: neither is defined without a true value to compare against, and Type M divides by it. Their interval and standard error are NaN then too, and type_m_mcse is also NaN when a single replicate reached significance, since a standard deviation needs two.

Details

The t-test treats every row as an independent observation, which is valid only when each subject contributes one row and no rows share a cluster. power_design() therefore takes a Gaussian design with exactly one two-level factor between subjects and no item unit, within factor or grouping factor besides subject. Continuous predictors and by-subject random effects are allowed, since with one row per subject they vary independently from row to row. Any other design is refused with a message naming what makes its rows correlated. power_mixed() fits the model that such a design implies. Take 30 subjects crossed with 20 items, with by-subject and residual standard deviations of 1 and a by-item one of 0.3. With no true effect, a t-test of every row is significant in about half of all replicates.

Each level of the factor needs at least two subjects, so a design needs at least 4. The subjects are split into two blocks in level order, and the second level holds floor(N / 2). With one subject at a level, the pooled variance rests on the other level alone, and with one at each it has no degree of freedom at all.

A specification with no coefficient for the factor's contrast has a true effect of 0, so type_s and type_m are NaN.

Power, Type S and Type M are each estimated from a finite number of replicates, so each is reported with its Monte Carlo error. Power has its standard error and a 95% Wilson interval, one of the intervals Brown, Cai and DasGupta (2001) recommend in place of the Wald interval. It stays between 0 and 1 and does not shrink to a point when power is 0 or 1. Type S and Type M rest on the significant replicates alone, often a handful. Type S has a Wilson interval, because its standard error is zero whenever no sign is wrong. Type M has its standard error, the standard deviation of the exaggeration ratios over the square root of their number.

A directional prediction calls for a one-sided test, which alternative selects. The estimate is the mean of the second level minus that of the first, whose true value is true_effect. "greater" tests whether it is positive and "less" whether it is negative, by stats::t.test() with the same alternative. The one-sided p-value is half the two-sided one when the estimate lies in the tested direction. A one-sided test at alpha therefore rejects in exactly the replicates in which the two-sided test at 2 * alpha rejects with the estimate in that direction. Type S and Type M are taken over the replicates significant in the tested direction. When that is the direction of the true effect, Type S is 0 by construction, and Type M is the exaggeration among the replicates that would support the prediction.

Results from earlier versions were two-sided. A one-sided power at alpha, in the direction of the true effect, can be read off a two-sided result at 2 * alpha: it is power * (1 - type_s). Type M is recovered only when that result's Type S is 0, since the wrong-signed replicates cannot otherwise be told apart from the others.

References

Brown, L. D., Cai, T. T. and DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a binomial proportion. Statistical Science, 16(2), 101-133. doi:10.1214/ss/1009213286

Gelman, A. and Carlin, J. (2014). Beyond power calculations: Assessing Type S (sign) and Type M (magnitude) errors. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9(6), 641-651. doi:10.1177/1745691614551642

Examples

spec <- build_spec(list(name = "d", seed = 1, design_kind = "between",
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b", n_subject = 64,
  intercept = 100, effect = 5, family = "gaussian", resp_name = "", sigma = 10))
# n_sims is small so the example runs quickly. Use 200 or more for real planning.
power_design(spec, n_sims = 50)

#> [1] 50
#> 
#> $alpha
#> [1] 0.05
#> 
#> $alternative
#> [1] "two.sided"

#> $power_mcse

#> 
#> $power_lo

#> 
#> $power_hi
#> [1] 0.6520286
#> 
#> $n_significant
#> [1] 26
#> 
#> $true_effect
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $mean_estimate
#> [1] 4.801842
#> 
#> $type_s
#> [1] 0
#>

#>
